title: The Stone That Walked

evidence.name: Two Clean Smears
evidence.text: The plinth in the visitor centre is dusty except for two long, tidy smears, as if a trolley's lip had slid the stone off. No scratches anywhere. Whoever took it cared about not damaging it.

evidence.name: Trolley Track
evidence.text: On the path from the centre, narrow rubber wheel marks, deep from a load. They head for the Vane Estates marquee, not the car park.

evidence.name: White Petals
evidence.text: Scraps of white paper confetti by the plinth. The biodegradable kind that venues insist on. Not the sort of thing you sell in a keyring shop.

evidence.name: Corky's Receipts
evidence.text: Corky Dunlop's stall books show 200 'genuine Causeway' keyring stones delivered from a Ballymoney gravel yard on Tuesday. Rounded pebbles, not hexagons. Shabby, but he has no use for a 60 kilo column.

evidence.name: Coleraine Library Slip
evidence.text: A late-fee slip in Dr Gault's notebook, stamped in Coleraine at 8.40 on Tuesday evening, for a book on columnar jointing. The stone went missing while she was queueing to pay 40p.

evidence.name: The Doorstep Request
evidence.text: The ranger's log: in March, Gerard Mullan asked to buy one basalt column 'for a doorstep'. Refused. Suspicious on paper, but his guest book has a Tuesday night complaint about his snoring until two, so he was in all night.

evidence.name: Saturday's Run Sheet
evidence.text: A wedding run sheet pinned in the marquee: '3pm, Item 4: bride and groom touch the Stone of Fionn for luck, photographs. Provide stone.' Signed F. Crozier, Events.

evidence.name: Trolley Hire Slip
evidence.text: The caterer's sack trolley was signed out on Tuesday teatime by F. Crozier and came back on Wednesday with grit in the wheels.

evidence.name: Table One
evidence.text: Under a long white cloth on the bride's table, a hexagonal basalt column about knee high, with a luggage label tied round it: 'TABLE 1. DO NOT USE AS A CHAIR.'

suspects.name: Corky Dunlop
suspects.wrong: A stone? Me? I sell keyrings! If I could carry sixty kilos I'd be in the army, not standing in a wind tunnel selling pebbles to Germans. I'm telling Mammy.

suspects.name: Dr Hilary Gault
suspects.wrong: I measured the thing, I did not abduct it. Columnar jointing is a lifelong love, not a criminal tendency. I shall be writing to the Geological Society, and they write back slowly and with footnotes.

suspects.name: Gerard Mullan
suspects.wrong: I only ASKED for one! In March! And I was told no, politely, which is how I knew it was serious. I have a guest book with a complaint about my snoring. I'd say that's an alibi, wouldn't you?

suspects.name: Fidelma Crozier
suspects.right: Oh, for goodness' sake. Saturday's bride wanted the Stone of Fionn in the photographs and I could not get a quote for a prop in under three weeks. I was going to put it back on Sunday. On a trolley. With a blanket. I'll pay for the trolley, and the apology, and the wedding will have to have a very nice plastic one.

steps.text: Speak to Ranger Boyle in the visitor centre at the Giant's Causeway.
Examine the empty plinth in the visitor centre.
Follow the wheel marks on the path outside the centre.
Question Corky Dunlop at his stall at the Causeway.
Question Dr Hilary Gault, the geologist, at the Causeway.
Ask the caterer in the Vane Estates marquee about Tuesday night.
Read the wedding run sheet in the marquee.
Talk to the events manager in the marquee.
Look under the cloth on the bride's table in the marquee.
Report back to Ranger Boyle in the visitor centre.

accuse_hint: Ranger Boyle is waiting in the visitor centre at the Giant's Causeway.
closed: The Stone of Fionn is back on its plinth, with a new sign asking visitors not to use it as a chair. Most of them will.
